design_detail: Case study of US newspaper coverage: a cross-sectional search and content analysis of the online archives of the 50 largest US newspapers with available archives, for stories on the September 2002 publication of a primate study reporting MDMA-induced dopaminergic neurotoxicity (Ricaurte et al., 2002) and on its September 2003 retraction. The units are newspapers (50) and stories, not people. Analyses: proportions of newspapers covering each event, word counts, Fisher's exact tests comparing retraction stories between newspapers that covered both events (14) and those that covered only the retraction (6), and simple logistic regression of coverage on circulation. The PDF is the online-first version (published online 26 November 2020): a publisher's cover page, then the article numbered pp. 1-7; the 2021 issue prints it as pp. 104-110 (issue pagination not checked). Anchors cite the online-first PDF's own page numbers. The 2002 paper and its retraction notice are not in this batch; what this article says about them is its authors' description.
can_establish: How many of these 50 newspapers ran stories on the publication and on the retraction, how long the stories were, and which elements the retraction stories contained, as coded by the authors.
cannot_establish: Why coverage differed, whether the coverage influenced legislation or research, how the public understood either event, or anything about the effects of MDMA on the brain.

sample.recruitment: Newspapers, not people: the 50 largest US newspapers for which online archives were available through Newspapers.com or the newspapers' own websites, taken in order from a 2007 circulation list (Infoplease, 2007); because some lacked archives, the list was descended to rank 64 (Methods, 1st paragraph, pp. 2-3; Table 1, p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Newspapers without available online archives were skipped and replaced by the next largest.
sample.demographics: Not applicable; Table 1 lists the 50 newspapers in order of circulation.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Editors' calculation: 14 of the 64 largest newspapers were skipped for lack of archives.
sample.selection_effects: The frame is a 2007 ranking applied to coverage in 2002-2003, and newspapers without online archives were left out; the authors list their inability to search all of the 50 largest newspapers as a limitation (Discussion, 7th paragraph, p. 5). Television, magazines, wire services and online media are outside the frame, and where in each paper a story appeared was not analysed.

exposure.measurement: The events covered: the September 2002 publication and the September 2003 retraction. Stories were found by archive searches combining the terms MDMA, ecstasy, Ricaurte, monkey, dopamine, Johns Hopkins and retraction; where these found nothing, all articles mentioning MDMA or ecstasy from September to November 2002 and September to November 2003 were read (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 3).

comparison.controls: Coverage of the publication compared with coverage of the retraction in the same 50 newspapers; the content of retraction stories compared between the 14 newspapers that covered both events and the 6 that covered only the retraction.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense. Newspaper characteristics that could explain coverage (science staff, use of wire stories, editorial policy) were not recorded; only circulation was tested.

outcomes.instruments: Whether each newspaper ran a story on each event; word counts; a content analysis of the 20 retraction stories for 17 reporting components (Table 2, p. 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: No coding manual, coder description, blinding or inter-rater reliability is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Retraction reporting is called balanced (Abstract; Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 5) without a definition; lack of context is judged from which of the 17 components a story contained.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 15 Fisher's exact comparisons (two components were present in every story), none significant, the lowest p being 0.06.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the coders are not identified.

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions without confidence intervals: publication covered by 26 of 50 newspapers (52%; editors' calculation, Wilson 95% CI 38.5% to 65.2%) and the retraction by 20 of 50 (40%; 27.6% to 53.8%); 14 of the 26 newspapers that covered the publication covered the retraction (54%; 35.5% to 71.2%). The publication-versus-retraction difference is not tested; editors' calculation from the discordant newspapers (12 covered only the publication, 6 only the retraction): exact McNemar p=0.24. Mean word counts 482 (SD 303) for publication stories and 396 (SD 193) for retraction stories, not tested; editors' calculation, Welch t=1.17, p=0.25, treating the stories as independent. Circulation was not associated with coverage of the publication (p=.25) or of the retraction (p=.84); no coefficients are given.
analysis.selective_reporting: The 14-of-26 figure conditions on newspapers that had already covered the publication; the symmetric figure, that 14 of the 20 newspapers covering the retraction (70%) had covered the publication (editors' calculation), is not given. The underlying data are available from the first author on request (Data availability statement, p. 5).
analysis.power: Not discussed. With 14 against 6 newspapers in the content comparison, only very large differences could have been detected.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A few more of these 50 newspapers covered the publication (26) than the retraction (20); about half of those that had covered the publication (14 of 26) also covered the retraction, while 6 covered only the retraction. Retraction stories were somewhat shorter on average, with wide spread. Every retraction story reported that the original findings had suggested one night's use could cause brain damage or parkinsonism and that a mix-up of compounds made them erroneous. None of the publication-versus-retraction differences was tested, and the content comparison found no significant difference.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the overall decrease moderate and the lower retraction coverage among newspapers that had covered the publication concerning, and calls retraction stories balanced. The discussion explains the difference by the sensational AAAS press release, the parkinsonism angle, the media narrative of the time and the late-Friday release of the retraction, none of which was tested, and closes by suggesting that sensational coverage of the erroneous findings may have slowed the development of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 5). It also states, citing only a 2014 commentary by Doblin and colleagues for the regulatory point, that evidence of dopaminergic toxicity of MDMA in humans has not materialized since the retraction (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 5). The second author directs the organization that sponsors the Phase 3 trials the discussion mentions. The same causal suggestion frames the study's rationale: the Introduction says the 2002 publication may have influenced the passage of anti-drug legislation aimed at recreational MDMA use and slowed efforts to gain regulatory approval for MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (p. 2), sourced to the sponsoring organization's own documents and a journal editorial. The abstract also states that the retraction stories were balanced but shorter, which the paper does not test.

timeline.event: Publication of the primate study (Ricaurte et al., 2002), with a university announcement and an AAAS press release (as described here, p. 2).
Letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin criticizing the study, and the authors' reply (June 2003).
Retraction (September 2003), as described here: methamphetamine instead of MDMA given to all but one animal because of a labelling error.
Earlier case study of the media coverage of another retracted paper (Rada, 2005, as cited; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: A single descriptive case study; the authors compare it with one earlier case study and a survey of retraction coverage (Rada, 2005, 2007), neither read here.

funding.declared_conflicts: Disclosure statement (p. 5): Dr. Barnett has received no funding from pharmaceutical companies or organizations involved in MDMA therapeutic research; Dr. Doblin is the founder and executive director of the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS), which funds research assessing the therapeutic potential of MDMA and other psychedelic compounds.
funding.affiliations_note: Barnett: Cleveland Clinic, Ohio; Doblin: MAPS, Santa Cruz, California. As the article itself reports, MAPS criticized the original study, asked NIDA to investigate and obtained the released documents (p. 2), and sponsors the Phase 3 trials mentioned in the discussion (p. 5); Doblin also co-wrote one of the 2003 letters criticizing the study (card sc_mithoefer_2003). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the counts.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered content analysis of the coverage of many retracted and comparable non-retracted studies, with archive searches checked against a second source, two independent coders unaware of the hypothesis, reliability statistics, and paired tests with intervals for the publication-versus-retraction difference.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Large US newspapers are a reasonable frame for print coverage, but the ranking is from 2007 rather than 2002-2003 and papers without online archives were replaced by smaller ones.
A census of the largest newspapers with archives rather than a sample; whether lack of archives is related to coverage is unknown (14 of the top 64 skipped, editors' calculation).
Fifty newspapers give proportions with intervals of roughly 14 percentage points either way; the content comparison of 14 against 6 newspapers is far too small for its tests.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 lists the newspapers; the archive sources and search terms are given.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 50 newspapers were searched and every retraction story was coded.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Keyword archive searches with a manual fallback for two three-month windows; the sensitivity of the searches was not checked; no search date and no second searcher are reported.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: No coding scheme, coders, blinding or inter-rater reliability are reported for the content analysis, and balanced reporting is not defined.

The main comparison (publication against retraction coverage, paired by newspaper) and the word-count difference are not tested and no intervals are given; 15 uncorrected Fisher tests compare 14 with 6 newspapers.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: No response rate applies; the availability of archives is covered under items 1 and 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The counts are simple and probably close to right for these 50 newspapers, but the searches were not validated, the content coding is unreported, the coders are not named although both authors' affiliations bear on the topic, and the central comparison was not tested. The counts may be cited as a description of these newspapers' coverage; the judgments of balance and the explanations for the difference may not. What the article says about the 2002 study and its retraction is second-hand and should be cited as its description.

key_findings.finding: As the article describes the original study: published in Science in September 2002 by Ricaurte, McCann and colleagues at Johns Hopkins University, funded by NIDA, in which MDMA was given to 10 non-human primates to model human use; the authors report that it found severe dopaminergic and less severe serotonergic neurotoxicity and that two of the animals died, and that the dopaminergic finding was new and raised the possibility of parkinsonism.
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the 2002 paper was not read. The authors of the 2002 study wrote in 2003 that one of ten monkeys died (card sc_mithoefer_2003).

key_findings.finding: As described: the Johns Hopkins Gazette announced that the researchers had found extensive damage to brain dopamine neurons in primates at doses it likened to those young adults take at all-night dance parties; the AAAS press release was titled as a study finding that ecstasy causes brain damage and closed with its chief executive likening use to Russian roulette with brain function; the New York Times wrote that the amount some take in a single night may cause permanent brain damage. MAPS and Mithoefer et al. (2003) criticized the findings, and Ricaurte et al. defended them, saying their results differed from earlier studies because of a novel protocol.

As described: in September 2003, one year after publication, Science issued a retraction in which Ricaurte and colleagues wrote that methamphetamine rather than MDMA had been used to treat all but one study animal, because of a labelling error (Ricaurte et al., 2003b); MAPS then asked NIDA to investigate all work done by the group since the mislabelled supply was received.
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the retraction notice was not read.

key_findings.finding: As described: NIDA issued no report, but in January 2004, in response to a Freedom of Information Act request by MAPS, released documents listing affected projects and indicating that another article would be retracted; a Nature editorial noted that the publication had received far more US media coverage than the retraction and discussed its possible influence on the passage of the Illicit Drug Anti-Proliferation Act; MAPS reported that a psychotherapy trial in Spain was shut down and approval efforts in the United States hampered.

Of 50 newspapers, 26 (52%) ran a story on the publication and 20 (40%) on the retraction; 6 (12%) covered the retraction without having covered the publication; of the 26 that covered the publication, 14 (54%) covered the retraction. Circulation was not associated with coverage of the publication (p=.25) or of the retraction (p=.84).

Mean word count 482 (SD 303; range 69-1260) for publication stories and 396 (SD 193; 86-837) for retraction stories. In newspapers covering both events, 550 (SD 271; 188-1260) against 386 (SD 205; 86-837); publication-only newspapers 404 (SD 331; 69-1038); retraction-only newspapers 420 (SD 177; 124-652).
key_findings.note: Editors' check: the subgroup means recombine to the overall means (14 x 550 + 12 x 404 over 26 gives 483; 14 x 386 + 6 x 420 over 20 gives 396).

key_findings.finding: All 20 retraction stories reported that the original findings had suggested that one night's MDMA use could cause brain damage or parkinsonism and that a mix-up of study compounds made the results erroneous; 14 (70%) mentioned long-standing scientific controversy, 13 (65%) earlier criticism, 11 (55%) that animals died, 11 (55%) that the laboratory blamed its supplier, 8 (40%) McCann's regrets, 7 (35%) earlier research suggesting serotonergic damage, 7 (35%) allegations of political motives, 5 (25%) NIDA funding; 4 (20%) each a critic's quotation, the laboratory's statement that its earlier MDMA findings were unaffected, the university's statement that Ricaurte remained in good standing, McCann's continuing concerns about MDMA, and Ricaurte's statement that the laboratory had not verified the compounds; 3 (15%) his denial of political influence; 2 (10%) that Leshner had defended the findings. No component differed significantly between the 14 and the 6 newspapers (Fisher's exact test, p from 0.06 to 1.00).
key_findings.note: Editors' check: every percentage in Table 2 matches its count, and the Fisher p values recomputed for five rows (0.06, 0.16, 0.27, 0.35, 0.61) agree.

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the retraction stories balanced but often short of context, such as quotations from the study's authors or critics, the allegations of political influence, and earlier research suggesting serotonergic damage after recreational use.

The authors state that debate continues over whether serotonergic damage associated with recreational use applies to pharmaceutical-grade MDMA (citing Doblin et al., 2014, and Parrott, 2013, 2014) and over long-term neurocognitive deficits (citing among others Parrott, 2011, Lyvers, 2011, and Halpern et al., 2004, 2011), and that evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not materialized since the retraction.
key_findings.note: An assertion without citation of human studies; the source given for the regulatory point is a commentary (Doblin et al., 2014). The Parrott (2013) cited here is a different paper (Human Psychopharmacology 28:289-307, per the reference list) from the review carded in this batch as parrott_2013.

key_findings.finding: Limitations given by the authors: archives could not be searched for all of the 50 largest US newspapers, the AAAS press release for the retraction could not be obtained, and the placement of stories within newspapers was not analysed. As quoted from a Nature editorial, the retraction was issued late on Friday 5 September, giving low-key coverage.

reporting_issues.issue: The article says two of the primates died, whereas the authors of the 2002 study wrote in their 2003 reply that one of ten monkeys given the regimen died of complications related to hyperthermia (Mithoefer et al., 2003, p. 1504).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of deaths should not be cited from either source without the original paper or its retraction notice.

reporting_issues.issue: The 14-of-26 figure (newspapers covering the publication that also covered the retraction) is framed as much lower retraction coverage, but it conditions on having covered the publication; the symmetric figure, 14 of the 20 newspapers covering the retraction (70%) having covered the publication, is not reported (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline contrast is partly a product of how the subset was chosen; the untested 52% against 40% is the fair comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference list gives Parrott (2011) as Addiction 106:1365-1268 and Fisk et al. (2011) as Addiction 106:1268-69; the PDF of Parrott (2011) shows that letter at pp. 1365-1368 and the Fisk et al. letter beginning on p. 1368.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation errors; use the DOIs.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name the archive sources and the search terms and describe a manual search of two three-month windows as a fallback, but give no date on which the archives were searched and no second searcher or verification of the searches.
reporting_issues.consequence: The counts, which are the only part of this study the encyclopedia cites, cannot be reproduced against the same archive state, and single-searcher coverage cannot be checked (JBI item 6).
